title: A form of refined Roth's theorem and its application to the $abc$-conjecture

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Theorem 1.4 asserts, with no epsilon-term, that all but finitely many algebraic integers x satisfy (q-1)h(x) ≤ Σ N̄(x,a_j)+O(1) (the truncated counting functions of Conjecture 1.2). This is false: take κ=Q, S={∞}, q=2, a_1=0, a_2=1 and x=3^{2^n}. Then h(x)=2^n log3, N̄(x,0)=log3, and since 2^{n+2} | 3^{2^n}-1 we get N̄(x,1)=log rad(x-1) ≤ log(x-1)-(n+1)log2. Hence the right-hand side is ≤ h(x)-(n+1)log2+O(1) < h(x) for large n, contradicting (11). The asserted inequality is strictly stronger than the ε=0 form of the abc-conjecture, which is known to be false.

Theorem 1.6 claims max{|a|,|b|,|c|} ≤ C·r(abc) with an absolute constant C whenever one of a,b,c is squarefree. Counterexample family: a=1, b=3^{2^n}-1, c=3^{2^n} (a is trivially squarefree, gcd=1). Since v_2(3^{2^n}-1)=n+2, rad(abc) ≤ 3(3^{2^n}-1)/2^{n+1}, so max/rad ≥ 2^{n+1}/3 → ∞. Thus no absolute constant C exists; an abc-type inequality with exponent exactly 1 is known to fail (cf. the lower bounds of Stewart–Tijdeman, cited by the paper itself as [10]). Theorem 1.5, from which Theorem 1.6 is deduced, is false for the same reason.

predicted_errors.error_location: Proof of Theorem 1.4 ('By using Dirichlet's unit theorem ... |y|_v ≤ c(κ)|y|_w')
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The claim 'there exists a constant c(κ) such that |y|_v ≤ c(κ)|y|_w for any Archimedean v,w' for an arbitrary algebraic integer y is false. Dirichlet's unit theorem only allows one to replace y by a unit multiple whose archimedean absolute values are comparable; it says nothing about an arbitrary integer. E.g. in Q(√2), y=(1+√2)^n has |y|_v/|y|_w=(1+√2)^{2n}, unbounded. This false statement is the key step used to conclude m(x'Q(x),∞)=O(1), i.e. it is the load-bearing step of the whole paper.

predicted_errors.error_location: Proof of Theorem 1.4, line 'm(y, 0) = ∑_{w ∈ S} log^+ (1/‖y‖_w) + O(1) = O(1)'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The sum defining m(y,0) runs over all w ∈ S, including non-Archimedean places of S. For an algebraic integer y the terms log^+(1/‖y‖_w) at non-Archimedean w ∈ S are nonnegative and can be arbitrarily large (y may be divisible by high powers of primes in S). The argument only (incorrectly) addresses Archimedean places and gives no bound at all for the finite places of S, so the conclusion m(y,0)=O(1) does not follow.

predicted_errors.error_location: Theorem 2.1 statement and the construction of x' at the end of its proof / Remark
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Theorem 2.1 asserts 'There exist an extension field K of κ and an element x' ∈ K such that all but finitely many x ∈ κ satisfy (14)', i.e. a single x' valid for every x. However the construction (both in K and in the Remark) builds x'=x_0/x_∞ from the ideals a_0 = ∏ p_i^{r_i-1} and a_∞ = ∏ Q_i^{u_i+1} which are defined from the prime factorizations of x and of x−a_j; thus x' depends on x. The quantifier order in the statement is therefore wrong, and all the 'O(1)' constants that involve x' (e.g. c_v in (17)) are not uniform in x.

Inequality (16) contains the untruncated counting functions N(x,∞), N(x,a_j) and the term −N_{x'}(x), whereas (19) suddenly has the truncated functions N̄(x,∞), N̄(x,a_j) and no −N_{x'}(x). The identity −N_{x'}(x) = (N̄(x,∞)−N(x,∞)) + Σ_j(N̄(x,a_j)−N(x,a_j)), which would be needed, is never stated or proved, and it depends on the specific (x-dependent) construction of x' given only afterwards. The passage from (16) to (19) is therefore unjustified as written.

predicted_errors.error_location: Proof of Theorem 2.1, displayed lower bound for |Q(x)|_v
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The displayed bound |Q(x)|_v > (|A_j|_v/|x−a_j|_v){1 − (q−1)(δ_v/2q)/(δ_v(1−1/2q))} does not follow from the definitions: the set E_{vj} was defined with the threshold δ_v/(2ϰ_v) where ϰ_v = 1/2+(q−1)σ_v/ρ_v, not δ_v/(2q), and the ratio |A_i/A_j|_v (bounded by σ_v/ρ_v, which need not be ≤ 1) has been silently dropped. The correct computation must keep ϰ_v and the factor σ_v/ρ_v.

predicted_errors.error_location: Proof of Theorem 2.1, last case of the proof of (17) ('If |x − a_i|_v > δ_v/2 for all i')
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The estimate ∏_j |x'/(x−a_j)|_{v+} ≤ (2/δ_v)_+^q omits the factor |x'|_v: one only has |x'/(x−a_j)|_{v+} ≤ max{1, 2|x'|_v/δ_v}. Since |x'|_v is unbounded (and x' itself depends on x), the asserted constant c_v in (17) cannot be chosen independently of x, which is required for the O(1) in (18).

predicted_errors.error_location: Proof of Theorem 1.5 ('Since x is simple, y = 1/(x'Q(x)) is an algebraic integer')
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: For a simple (non-integral) x, 1/Q(x)=(x−a_1)(x−a_2) has denominator supported on all primes of the denominator of x, including those in S, while the constructed x_∞ generates a_∞ = ∏_{i≤h} Q_i^{u_i+1} built only from primes Q_i ∈ M_κ − S. Hence x'Q(x)^{-1} is at best an S-integer, not an algebraic integer, and the subsequent argument (copied from Theorem 1.4) does not apply.

References [1], [2], [3] and [4] are cited repeatedly in the text (e.g. 'S. Lang [4] observed', '(see [3], Theorem 6.14)', '(see [3], p. 358)', '[3], Theorem 2.32', 'Theorem 2.36 and Lemma 4.3 in [3]', 'Section 5.6.1 in [3]', 'can be found in [1], [8] ... see also [2]'), but the reference list begins with [5]; these four sources are entirely missing, making the central citations (including the two results on which key steps rely) unverifiable.

predicted_errors.error_location: Theorem 1.4 (Eq. (11)) vs. end of its proof (Eq. (20))
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Theorem 1.4 states (q−1)h(x) ≤ Σ_j N(x,a_j)+O(1), but the proof concludes with (20): (q−1)h(x) ≤ N(x,∞)+Σ_j N(x,a_j)+O(1), which contains an extra term N(x,∞) not present in the theorem. Moreover the counting functions are written without the bar in (11), (12), (16), (20) but with the bar (truncated) in (9), (14), (19), (21); since the entire point of the paper is the truncated version, this notational inconsistency makes the statements ambiguous and inconsistent with each other.

predicted_errors.error_location: Proof of Theorem 1.6 (text after Theorem 1.5, 'Since a + b + c = 0')
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Conjecture 1.3 and Theorem 1.6 are stated for a + b = c, but the proof uses the relation a + b + c = 0 and correspondingly evaluates N̄(a/c, −1) (which equals the b-contribution only under a+b+c=0). Under the stated hypothesis a+b=c one has a/c − 1 = −b/c, so the target should be +1. The two conventions are mixed without comment.

predicted_errors.error_location: Introduction, 'Some results that would follow from the abc-conjecture can be found in [1], [8], pp. 185-188, [14]; see also [2], [5], [6], [15]'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Reference [6] is Lang's 'Algebra' (a general graduate algebra textbook), which contains no results depending on or related to the abc-conjecture; citing it as a source for consequences of the abc-conjecture is a misattribution (presumably a different Lang title was intended).

predicted_errors.error_location: Theorem 2.1 statement ('and ε a positive constant')
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: A positive constant ε is introduced as a hypothesis of Theorem 2.1 but never occurs in the conclusion (14) nor anywhere in the proof; the hypothesis is vacuous and misleading (it suggests an ε-dependence of the stated inequality that does not exist).

predicted_errors.error_location: Proof of Theorem 2.1, 'Thus there exist x_0, x_∞ ∈ O_K such that (x_0)=O_K a_0, (x_∞)=O_K a_∞'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The ideals a_0 and a_∞ are used here without ever having been defined in the proof; they are only introduced later, inside the Remark, in terms of the prime factorizations of x and x−a_j. As written the definition of x' (and hence the whole error-term analysis) is circular/undefined at the point of use.

predicted_errors.error_location: Remark, 'If p_1,...,p_{m_q} are not distinct, say p_1 = p_2 ... replace δ_2 by p_1^{r_1} p_2^{r_2} δ_2 = a_0 p_1 ⋯ p_{m_q}'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: This display equates an element (δ_2) multiplied by prime powers with an ideal, which is meaningless; presumably the ideal d_2 was meant. Also 'Since d_i | δ_i, hence p_j | δ_i (j≠i)' should read p_j^{r_j} | δ_i. These steps as written do not establish the asserted divisibility properties of x_0.

predicted_errors.error_location: Transition from Theorem 2.1 (a_j ∈ κ) to Theorems 1.4/1.5 (a_j ∈ κ̄)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Theorems 1.4 and 1.5 are stated for distinct a_j ∈ κ̄, but Theorem 2.1, from which they are deduced, requires a_j ∈ κ. The only remark offered ('if (11) is true for all algebraic integers a_j, then it is true for all algebraic numbers a_j') concerns integrality, not membership in the base field, and is moreover placed inside the proof of Theorem 2.1, referring forward to the statement being proved.
